tip: 'paid â' plus a verb tells one person not to do something: 'paid â stopio' = don't stop.
'po fwyaf' before each half frames the more...the more: 'po fwyaf dw i'n dysgu' = the more I learn.
'fy' (my) triggers a nasal change in the next word: 'tad-cu' turns into 'fy nhad-cu' (t to nh).
'na' (than) puts an h after c, p and t: 'cyfoeth' becomes 'na chyfoeth' (c to ch).
better is the irregular 'gwell', not 'mwy da': 'yn well na'r llynedd' = better than last year.
higher is the irregular 'uwch', from 'uchel': 'yn uwch na'r bryn' = higher than the hill.
add '-ach' for -er or more: 'tawel' (quiet) becomes 'tawelach', softened to 'dawelach' after 'yn'.
'i' (to) softens place names: 'Caerfyrddin' becomes 'i Gaerfyrddin' (c to g).
a feminine noun softens the adjective after it: 'gêm' plus 'cyfartal' gives 'gêm gyfartal'.
'o' (of or from) softens the next word: 'gwledydd' becomes 'o wledydd' (drops g).
in Wales is 'yng Nghymru': 'yn' shifts to 'yng' and 'Cymru' takes a nasal change to 'Nghymru'.
'na' becomes 'nag' before a vowel: 'ddyfnach nag oeddwn' = deeper than I was.
'lle' links a place to a clause, meaning where: 'fferm lle maen nhw'n gwneud' = the farm where they make.
'pe bawn i' means if I were: 'pe bawn i'n ennill mwy' = if I earned more.
add '-af' for the most: 'byr' (short) becomes 'byrraf' (shortest), doubling the r.
adjectives usually follow the noun in Welsh: 'band eang gwell' reads broadband better, meaning better broadband.
'pe bai' sets up an unreal if, answered by 'byddwn i'n' (I would): 'pe bai mwy o amser..., byddwn i'n dysgu'.
bad has an irregular worst form: 'drwg' becomes 'gwaethaf', softened to 'ffilm waethaf' here.
the linking 'yn' softens a following noun too: 'canwr' becomes 'yn ganwr' = a singer (c to g).
older is the irregular 'hŷn', from 'hen': 'fy mrawd yn hŷn na fi' = my brother is older than me.
three shows gender: 'tair' with feminine nouns, 'tri' with masculine; here 'tair ochr' = three sides.
for longer adjectives use 'mwyaf' before the word instead of an '-af' ending: 'mwyaf poblogaidd' = most popular.
'sy'n' means who or that is, joining a doer to an action: 'rieni sy'n gweithio' = parents who work.
best has an irregular form 'gorau', from 'da', never 'daaf': 'y gorau' = the best.
'bod' means that after verbs of saying or seeming: 'mae'n ymddangos bod pethau'n newid' = it seems things change.
a past unreal if adds 'wedi': 'pe bai mwy o adnoddau wedi'u dyrannu' = if more had been allocated, not were.
'fy' (my) triggers a nasal change: 'coesau' turns into 'fy nghoesau' (my legs), c becoming ngh.
the '-odd' ending marks a he/she past tense: 'hedfan' (to fly) becomes 'hedfanodd' (flew).
'drwy' (through) softens the next word: 'Cymru' becomes 'drwy Gymru', c changing to g.
after 'fy' (my) the next word takes a nasal change: 'tad-cu' becomes 'fy nhad-cu' here, t shifting to nh.
